title: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet
shortTitle: What is the difference between HashSet and LinkedHashSet?

s1_definition.profdef: `HashSet` stores unique elements with no ordering guarantee and offers O(1) average add, remove and contains. `LinkedHashSet` extends HashSet and additionally maintains a doubly linked list across all entries, so iteration returns elements in INSERTION order while keeping the same O(1) operations. The trade-off is that LinkedHashSet uses slightly more memory for the two extra pointers per entry.
s1_definition.analogy: HashSet is like throwing unique cheques into a drawer — no duplicates, but you cannot predict the order you pull them out. LinkedHashSet is the same drawer with a thread tying the cheques together in the exact order you dropped them in, so you always read them back in arrival order.
s1_definition.oneliner: HashSet is unordered O(1); LinkedHashSet is insertion-ordered O(1) at the cost of extra pointers.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `HashSet` stores unique elements with no ordering guarantee and offers O(1) average add, remove and contains. `LinkedHashSet` extends HashSet and additionally maintains a doubly linked list across all entries, so iteration returns elements in INSERTION order while keeping the same O(1) operations. The trade-off is that LinkedHashSet uses slightly more memory for the two extra pointers per entry.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** HashSet is like throwing unique cheques into a drawer — no duplicates, but you cannot predict the order you pull them out. LinkedHashSet is the same drawer with a thread tying the cheques together in the exact order you dropped them in, so you always read them back in arrival order.

**One line to remember:** HashSet is unordered O(1); LinkedHashSet is insertion-ordered O(1) at the cost of extra pointers.

sections.s3_banking: At the National Bank of India this came up directly when handling HashSet versus LinkedHashSet. Rajesh holds savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees and Priya holds current account CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees, and the team needed the collection behaviour to be exactly correct so balances and account lists were never wrong. The runnable demo below reproduces the situation and proves the behaviour with a small test.

sections.s6_takeaway:
HashSet and LinkedHashSet both guarantee uniqueness with constant-time operations, but HashSet gives no ordering while LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order by maintaining a doubly linked list across its entries.

In the National Bank reporting module I used a HashSet when I only needed fast membership checks on account identifiers, and switched to a LinkedHashSet whenever the processed order mattered, for example listing the accounts Rajesh and Priya touched in the exact sequence the batch received them. The small extra memory for the linked pointers was well worth the deterministic, auditable output.

In an interview I would stress that I always use BigDecimal for money, keep map keys immutable, and pick the collection whose ordering and complexity match the banking access pattern, because in a system that moves real money, choosing the wrong data structure is not a style issue, it is a correctness and reliability issue.

keyPoints: HashSet: unordered — iteration order is unpredictable
LinkedHashSet: maintains insertion order via internal linked list
LinkedHashSet: slightly more memory but predictable iteration
